{"id": "104:2/q02", "question": "How is ٱلَّذِى connected grammatically to the preceding verse?", "turns_on": "Case and whether definiteness allows an adjectival link to kull; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī challenge the adjective analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q02/p1", "position": "It is a genitive appositive to kull or the preceding condemned person.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhās, al-Tabrisī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī give this parsing. Al-Samīn rejects treating it as an adjective or explanatory apposition because definiteness differs. Bursawī also denies adjective agreement."}, {"id": "104:2/q02/p2", "position": "It is accusative by an implied expression of censure or clarification.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says 'I mean'; al-Kashshāf and others call it accusative censure."}, {"id": "104:2/q02/p3", "position": "It is nominative with an implied subject or as a disjoined expression of blame.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās supplies 'he is'; al-Samīn calls it disjunction; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī call it nominative dispraise."}, {"id": "104:2/q02/p4", "position": "It is a partitive appositive to kull.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this as an alternative to full apposition."}, {"id": "104:2/q02/p5", "position": "It is another adjective describing the same slanderer.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the unlinked descriptions in 68:10–13. Al-Tabrisī mentions a codex variant; al-Jarbardī appeals to kull's definiteness and 50:21."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q03", "question": "What does the root of جَمَعَ convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q03/p1", "position": "It brings dispersed or varied things together, evoking massing, mingling, or assembly.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ surveys eighteen simple-verb occurrences and notes no Qur'anic derivative of its doubled form; thirteen concern God gathering people, bones or humanity for Judgment. She cites prayer, the Day of Gathering, goods, troops, weapons, and 4:23."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q04", "question": "How is جَمَعَ read and what does each form imply?", "turns_on": "Whether doubling adds sustained or abundant collection; the light form can also carry these senses, and reader attributions differ.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q04/p1", "position": "Jamaʿa has a light mīm; it means gathering and can itself describe either abundant or successive collection.", "reasons": "Read by ʿĀṣim, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and others, though lists vary. Abū ʿAmr associates it with much gathered; Abū ʿAlī permits itemwise gathering, supported by al-Aʿshā's equipment verse and 18:99. Al-Naḥḥās and al-Samīn allow little or much; al-Biqāʿī says collection itself suggests abundance. Ibn ʿĀshūr says intensive counting implies further amassing. Al-Nashr assigns the light mīm to all readers other than the six it names for the doubled form."}, {"id": "104:2/q04/p2", "position": "Jammaʿa has a doubled mīm; it intensifies gathering, often as repeated collection from different places or item by item.", "reasons": "Reader lists include Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī, with variants involving al-Ḥasan, Khalaf, Rūḥ or Ruways. Abū al-Ḥasan considers it apt for gathering from place to place; Abū ʿAmr distinguishes itemwise accumulation. Al-Kashshāf, al-Nasafī and others note its formal match with ʿaddadahu; Abū ʿUbayd prefers it for that reason. Al-Ṭabarī accepts both regional forms as close in meaning. Al-Nashr specifically names Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf, and Rawḥ as readers of the doubled mīm."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q05", "question": "What counts as مَالًۭا here?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is being defined by general usage or the man's reported holdings.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q05/p1", "position": "Acquired resources for needs, with the familiar form varying by livelihood: camels, gardens and palms, or trade money.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Zuhayr on camels as blood money, Abū Hurayra and Abū Ṭalḥa on Ansārī gardens and palms, the Prophet's question to al-ʿAbbās on Meccan cash, and earlier discussion at 3:92."}, {"id": "104:2/q05/p2", "position": "The man’s possessions include gold, silver, lands, gardens, slaves, servants and livestock.", "reasons": "Muqātil's narrative lists the inventoried property, preparation to purchase servants and livestock, and gardens in Mecca and Taif bearing fruit in winter and summer."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q06", "question": "Why is مَالًۭا indefinite?", "turns_on": "Whether indefiniteness enlarges the imagined amount or diminishes its worth.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q06/p1", "position": "It magnifies the amount or the wealth's corrupt, vile character.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives the latter account; al-Ālūsī gives magnification and cites competing reports that al-Akhnas had four or ten thousand dinars."}, {"id": "104:2/q06/p2", "position": "It belittles an individual's wealth as trivial before God or beside all worldly wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī invokes 18:46 and the whole world's wealth; al-Ālūsī calls it contemptible in God's sight; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it serves only brief bodily needs."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q07", "question": "How is وَعَدَّدَهُۥ read?", "turns_on": "Regional reading consensus and the written two dāls versus reports of lightening and whether the light form is a noun or exceptional verb.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q07/p1", "position": "The established or majority reading doubles the dāl, ʿaddadahu.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says all regional readers agree and rejects a weak early alternative for opposing that consensus. Al-Biqāʿī says undoubled counting can mean only a few things; doubled form emphasizes repetition or abundance. Al-Bayḍāwī notes a separated doubling as support."}, {"id": "104:2/q07/p2", "position": "A minority reading lightens the dāl; it can be parsed as a noun for number or an unusual separated verb meaning counted.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to al-Ḥasan, al-Kalbī, Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim, Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn Yaʿmar and al-Sulamī. Al-Ṭabarī rejects its transmission; al-Naḥḥās, al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī call verbal lightening remote or strained. Poetry with ḍannanū supports poetic license; al-Mahdawī instead parses a coordinated noun, avoiding irregularity."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q08", "question": "What does وَعَدَّدَهُۥ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether ʿaddadahu is intensive counting, provision from ʿuddah, increase in amount or kinds, or a coordinated noun for supporters; some explanations add heirs or boasting.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q08/p1", "position": "He counted and repeatedly inventoried his wealth, often guarding the amount from decrease.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash derives it from ʿidda; al-Farrāʾ, al-Suddī and many others gloss tallying. Mujāhid specifies types; ʿIkrima counts enough for years. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says guarding the sum prevented charity. Al-Suddī pictures saying 'this is mine' by day and hiding it at night; Ibn Kathīr cites 70:18. Al-Ālūsī says love drove repetition; al-Iṣlāḥī adds business forecasts and investment calculations. Al-Dāmghānī gives ʿidda the sense of number or count and illustrates it with months, sleepers, possessions, and people."}, {"id": "104:2/q08/p2", "position": "He stored or prepared wealth as a reserve for calamities or future need.", "reasons": "Muqātil invokes provision and storage; al-Naẓm derives ʿaddadahu from ʿuddah. Al-Baghawī cites Arabic aʿdadtu and ʿadadtuhu for keeping back. Al-Jubbāʾī adds unlawful acquisition and unpaid dues. Al-ʿĀṣim's rendering via al-Jawharī is 'counts it a safeguard.'"}, {"id": "104:2/q08/p3", "position": "He multiplied the quantity or kinds of wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Naẓm connects ʿadad/ʿadīd with largeness; al-Rāzī analogizes a numerous clan. Al-Ālūsī specifies real estate, goods and coins; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 3:14. Al-Wāḥidī also presents great quantity."}, {"id": "104:2/q08/p4", "position": "He gathered a numerous clan, followers, or supporters alongside wealth.", "reasons": "The light dāl can be a noun coordinated with māl; al-Kashshāf says a person of ʿadad has helpers and resources. Al-Rāzī connects this to pride. Al-Mahdawī prefers the noun analysis over poetic verbal de-gemination; al-Samīn identifies relatives. Al-Farrāʾ's gloss of the light reading includes clan."}, {"id": "104:2/q08/p5", "position": "He prepared the wealth for his children to inherit.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this possibility; al-Qurṭubī attributes it to al-Ḍaḥḥāk."}, {"id": "104:2/q08/p6", "position": "He boasted about the amount he owned.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī report this alternative; al-Iṣlāḥī describes calculation among flatterers."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q09", "question": "What is the force of counting the wealth?", "turns_on": "Whether attention falls on the hoarder's attachment and fear of loss or on the error of treating wealth as protection.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q09/p1", "position": "Repeated counting shows possessive love, obsessive calculation, and fear that the hoard will diminish.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he guards the sum and withholds charity; al-Suddī depicts daytime preoccupation and nighttime concealment; Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb depicts daylong piling and corpse-like sleep. Al-Ālūsī, Quṭb, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and al-Iṣlāḥī stress pleasure or anxious calculation."}, {"id": "104:2/q09/p2", "position": "Counting signals ignorance: wealth cannot protect against the calamities that divine wisdom uses to disperse it.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī and Bursawī connect counting with ignorance; Bursawī adds that accumulating reflects appetitive power."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q10", "question": "What does this description condemn?", "turns_on": "Which moral consequence of accumulation is foregrounded: unpaid duties, social arrogance, false security, or the warning's response.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q10/p1", "position": "Hoarding wealth, withholding its due and refusing charitable spending or obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says he fails to spend in God's path or pay God's due. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports al-Ṭabarī's reading."}, {"id": "104:2/q10/p2", "position": "Admiration of amassed wealth makes the slanderer imagine himself superior and belittle others.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Bursawī explain why this vice is singled out. Al-Biqāʿī says a culture that boasts of profit calls it success, while the verse exposes his loss; Ibn al-Zubayr links his imagined completeness and faultfinding to 103:2. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links perceived self-sufficiency and tyranny to 96:6–7; Quṭb portrays a recurring contemptuous type."}, {"id": "104:2/q10/p3", "position": "Trust in wealth to ward off death, judgment or hardship is delusion.", "reasons": "Quṭb says the hoarder thinks money secures life and evades God's decree; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says brief bodily needs and endless hope drive the illusion. Corpus Coranicum contrasts this hoarding with 90:6's showy spending, both seeking self-made immortality. Asad reads it as a safeguard."}, {"id": "104:2/q10/p4", "position": "The obsession and ridicule reveal a degraded character whom the warning and punishment answer.", "reasons": "Quṭb says the warning defends believers and pairs arrogance with the crushing Fire, reaching the heart, enclosure and pillars; harsh sound and an awe-inspiring question intensify it. He sees the Qur'an strengthening believers and striking opponents."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q11", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from collecting and counting wealth?", "turns_on": "The notes draw different spiritual lessons from wealth dependence and counting.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q11/p1", "position": "Wealth, status, kin or even obedience confer no true richness; relying on God alone does.", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī's anonymous sayings call the money-rich poor, status-rich contemptible, obedience-rich bankrupt and kin-rich lowly. Al-Qushayrī repeats dependence on wealth, rank and works as poverty or bankruptcy and says reliance on God gives nobility."}, {"id": "104:2/q11/p2", "position": "Accumulating, loving and hoarding wealth reveal spiritual ignorance, hypocrisy and unbelief.", "reasons": "An anonymous saying reported by al-Sulamī assigns these three diagnoses respectively; al-Tustarī says the miser makes wealth a servant of worldly life."}, {"id": "104:2/q11/p3", "position": "Ignorance is the root vice, and entrenched immersion in it leads to punishment that overwhelms the heart.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls ignorance a vice of the royal faculty and says the immersed merit eternal punishment; he also says counting wealth falsely assumes it can withstand calamity."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q12", "question": "What episode is reported behind the counting and condemnation?", "turns_on": "These are separate reported encounters; the notes do not say they describe the same event.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q12/p1", "position": "The man boasts that his wealth cannot be exhausted, is warned its Giver can take it, inventories it, then boasts to Muhammad; the sūra is revealed.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports the oath to distribute wealth through Quraysh, the warning of poverty, the inventory of gold, silver, land, gardens and slaves, and a boast that even as bread it would not run out."}, {"id": "104:2/q12/p2", "position": "Al-Ḥasan rebukes a wealthy visitor who saves thousands for hardship rather than helping others.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reports al-Ḥasan asking why the money ransoms no one and is given to no generous person; the visitor says it is for hardship, and al-Ḥasan predicts an ungrateful heir and an unforgiving Lord."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q13", "question": "How large was al-Akhnas's fortune in the reports?", "turns_on": "The reports give different numbers without a stated criterion for choosing one.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q13/p1", "position": "Four thousand dinars.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī preserve this report as one of two amounts."}, {"id": "104:2/q13/p2", "position": "Ten thousand dinars.", "reasons": "The same sources give this competing figure."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q14", "question": "How does this verse connect to surrounding passages and Qur'anic themes?", "turns_on": "The notes compare the verse with different neighboring and broader scriptural passages.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q14/p1", "position": "The wealth hoarder contrasts with al-ʿAṣr's call to truth, patience and recognition of human loss.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī's Ibn al-Zubayr cites 103:2; al-Iṣlāḥī cites 103:3 and says hoarders taunt those who press duties."}, {"id": "104:2/q14/p2", "position": "Other Qur'anic passages condemn hoarding, withholding and mockery of givers.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites 50:25 or 68:12 and 70:18; Ibn Kathīr cites 70:18; Study Quran cites 9:34–35's branding of hoarded gold and silver. Al-Iṣlāḥī reads 9:79 as hypocrites mocking poor donors while giving nothing."}, {"id": "104:2/q14/p3", "position": "The sūra's woe and vice catalogue resemble other Qur'anic warnings and prophetic woe speeches.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum cites 107:4–7, 83:1–6, 83:10–11, 52:11–12, 51:60 and Micah 2:1–3, highlighting the wealth theme and rhetorical question in 83:1–6."}, {"id": "104:2/q14/p4", "position": "The sūra condemns the hoarder in a Meccan nine-verse warning.", "reasons": "Quṭb identifies its place and length; Study Quran states its focus on torment for those who hoard in worldly life."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q15", "question": "Why render the perfect verbs as present actions?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q15/p1", "position": "Their perfect form is aspectual and describes a continuing type, warranting a German present tense.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum cites 96:1–2 for comparable aspectual use."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q16", "question": "Why might a translation repeat the opening woe at this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q16/p1", "position": "It treats the attitude in verses 2–3 as a separate blameworthy object beside the two kinds named in verse 1.", "reasons": "Asad explains his inserted repetition on this basis."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q17", "question": "What is reported about the seven named readings and their preservation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q17/p1", "position": "The seven named readings are sound choices of reciters within the ʿUthmānic codex tradition, not the Companions' seven aḥruf.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr transmits al-Qurṭubī citing al-Dāwūdī and Ibn Abī Ṣafra; reciters allowed one another's readings, choosing what seemed apt, and regional Muslims relied on soundly transmitted written documentation, fulfilling preservation."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q18", "question": "Who was Abū Zayd named among the collectors of the Qur'an?", "turns_on": "Anas's kinship and tribal claim and whether the named collector appears separately in al-Shaʿbī's list; Ibn Ḥajar finds an explicit report for Qays ibn al-Sakan.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q18/p1", "position": "Qays ibn al-Sakan of Banū ʿAdī ibn al-Najjār.", "reasons": "Ibn Ḥajar prefers the Ibn Abī Dāwūd report; Anas calls him his maternal uncle, says he died without descendants and Anas inherited him. Ibn Abī Dāwūd gives his lineage, ʿAqaba and Badr participation, and near-Prophetic death."}, {"id": "104:2/q18/p2", "position": "Saʿd ibn ʿUbayd ibn al-Nuʿmān of Banū ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf.", "reasons": "Al-ʿAskarī says Saʿd was the only Aws collector; Ibn Ḥabīb lists him as collecting in the Prophet's life. The identification is challenged because Anas was Khazrajī, called Abū Zayd an uncle, and al-Shaʿbī listed Saʿd separately."}, {"id": "104:2/q18/p3", "position": "Qays ibn Abī Saʿṣaʿa, a Khazrajī also called Abū Zayd.", "reasons": "Ibn Ḥajar offers this possibility because it fits Anas's kin claim."}, {"id": "104:2/q18/p4", "position": "Saʿd ibn al-Mundhir ibn Aws ibn Zuhayr, another Khazrajī collector.", "reasons": "Ibn Ḥajar names him but finds no explicit evidence of the kunya Abū Zayd."}, {"id": "104:2/q18/p5", "position": "Thābit, Aws or Muʿādh.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī lists these further proposed names without grounds."}]}
{"id": "104:2/q19", "question": "When were Qur'anic verses and surahs divided and ordered?", "turns_on": "Whether the complete surah sequence was fixed by revelation or partly arranged during codex production; the notes distinguish verse placement from surah order.", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q19/p1", "position": "Surahs and verse placement were established during the Prophet's lifetime.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās reports instructions to place a revealed verse in a named surah; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites known surah sizes, prophetic prayer recitations and marriage for memorized surahs. Al-Dānī says Gabriel showed placements, and Zayd reports arranging sheets before the Prophet, though al-Bayhaqī restricts this to verses."}, {"id": "104:2/q19/p2", "position": "The Prophet fixed the order of surahs.", "reasons": "Al-Bāqillānī lists this possibility; al-Dānī attributes verse and surah placement to Gabriel."}, {"id": "104:2/q19/p3", "position": "Some surah order was set in the Prophet's life, with remaining order fixed or preserved by Zayd and ʿUthmān.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya transmits al-Bāqillānī's strong view of Zayd and ʿUthmān; Ibn ʿĀshūr finds long opening surahs and Mufaṣṣal already placed, the rest uncertain. Zayd and ʿUthmān sought to preserve known prophetic recitation."}]}

{"id": "104:2/q22", "question": "Who else may gather around and count the wealth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:2/q22/p1", "position": "The slanderer's poorer companions may gather around him and count his wealth while aspiring to acquire their own through slander.", "reasons": "Elmalılı describes many in the humaza-lumaza circle as owning little, clustering around the wealthy man and counting his assets."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q01", "question": "What does yaḥsabu mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q01/p1", "position": "He supposes or falsely estimates that wealth has secured immortality.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭi distinguishes literal counting, figurative estimation, planning and divine reckoning; she says the Qurʾānic three-letter verb marks mistaken supposition, comparing the Queen of Sheba's mistake (27:44), 18:9 and 76:19. She surveys rebuking interrogatives at 29:2, 45:21, 47:29, 23:115, 29:4, 2:214, 3:142 and 9:16, and says all thirty-one open-vowel imperfect occurrences warn against misestimation. Al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguishes ḥasaba-yaḥsubu, 'to count,' from ḥasiba, 'to suppose'; Bint al-Shāṭi also notes ḥasab can mean inherited distinction."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q02", "question": "How is yaḥsabu read?", "turns_on": "The sīn vowel and the attested reciters or dialects; the notes say the sense is unchanged.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q02/p1", "position": "With fatḥa on the sīn, yaḥsabu.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this from al-Aʿraj, Abū Jaʿfar and Shayba; Ibn ʿĀshūr names Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and Abū Jaʿfar. Sibawayh calls ḥasiba-yaḥsabu sound and more analogical, though among exceptional imperfect vowels; he contrasts the three patterns shared by transitive and intransitive verbs with intransitive faʿula-yafʿulu, adduces al-Farazdaq's yanʿamu, faḍila-yafḍulu and māta-tamūtu, and relays al-Khalīl's judgment of kāda-takādu as irregular. His discussion of hamzated roots compares abā-yaʾbā with qaraʾa-yaqraʾu and ḥasiba-yaḥsabu, marks jabā-yajbā and qalā-yaqlā weakly transmitted, and cites better-attested ʿamara-yaʿmuru and yaḥzuru; he also discusses amara-yaʾmuru, akala-yaʾkulu, waʿadahu-yaʿiduhu and weak ʿaḍaḍtu-taʿaḍḍu by analogy. Al-Sāmarrāʾī calls this form more common in ordinary language. Both vocalizations mean 'supposes,' according to Qiraat-ER."}, {"id": "104:3/q02/p2", "position": "With kasra on the sīn, yaḥsibu.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās describes it as the Prophet's dialect on the rare faʿila-yafʿalu pattern. Al-Durr cites Jābir's report of the Prophet's pronunciation, authenticated by Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim and cited by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khaṭīb. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the majority reading and one of two dialectal forms; Qiraat-ER calls both canonical, with the same sense. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says every mutawātir reading may be recited in prayer and cites al-Jazarī's collection of ten in al-Nashr."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q03", "question": "How does the yaḥsabu sentence attach to what precedes?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause resumes, supplies the hoarder's circumstance, or implies a satirical question.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q03/p1", "position": "It is a new, independent sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr allow resumption; Ibn ʿĀshūr says an independent assertion can convey denial and taunt the hoarder."}, {"id": "104:3/q03/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause describing the hoarder.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says it can describe the subject of jamaʿa; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it satirically portrays the slanderer's greed."}, {"id": "104:3/q03/p3", "position": "An omitted interrogative makes it a taunting question.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the implicit question expresses mockery or amazement. Neuwirth once proposed inserting an explicit interrogative because four other early Meccan uses have one (75:3, 75:36, 90:5, 90:7) and 83:1–6 is a woe followed by a polemical question; Corpus Coranicum says she later seems to withdraw that emendation."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q04", "question": "What does the anna clause supply to yaḥsabu?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q04/p1", "position": "The anna clause and its governed words fill both objects of yaḥsabu.", "reasons": "This is al-Naḥḥās's syntactic analysis."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q05", "question": "Why repeat mālahu explicitly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q05/p1", "position": "Naming wealth where a pronoun could stand reinforces the point.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī and his full version give this as emphatic wording."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q06", "question": "What does akhladahu mean as a verb?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q06/p1", "position": "It means to cause someone to remain or live forever, or for a very long time.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī equate akhlada with khallada; al-Ālūsī allows unlimited or very long duration. Bint al-Shāṭi defines khuld as permanent endurance and says Qurʾānic worldly uses express illusion or deny human permanence: 21:34, 21:8, 26:129; she counts 87 root occurrences. {"id": "104:3/q07", "question": "What time does the past form akhladahu express?", "turns_on": "Whether completed wording projects a presumed future certainty or describes wealth's support up to now.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q07/p1", "position": "It presents the hoped-for future as already achieved.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī compare saying a sinner has perished or entered Hell before the consequence arrives. Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī say yaḥsabu makes the past verb prospective. Al-Rāzī, al-Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say the completed form depicts the hoarder's certainty as if survival were guaranteed; al-Ālūsī calls it intensification. Al-Ṭabrisī also says the cause can be described as an accomplished result before death occurs."}, {"id": "104:3/q07/p2", "position": "It retains a past sense: wealth has sustained or prolonged his life so far.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn expressly allows an actual past meaning. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say wealth has supported and protected his life, so he expects that support to continue; al-Qurṭubī reports the idea that it gave him life already, while also explaining a past-for-future use."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q08", "question": "Who is the agent and object of akhladahu?", "turns_on": "The grammatical subject and object of the causative verb; al-Ālūsī dismisses the inversion.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q08/p1", "position": "Wealth is the imagined agent and the man is its object.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the causative hamza this way; the normal interpretation throughout the commentaries takes wealth as what supposedly preserves its owner."}, {"id": "104:3/q08/p2", "position": "The man is the agent and wealth the object: he thinks he can keep his wealth forever.", "reasons": "ʿIṣām al-Dīn proposes this inversion; al-Ālūsī rejects it. {"id": "104:3/q09", "question": "What does the claim that wealth made him immortal mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the man's claim is literal, an illusion shown by his conduct, an extension or preservation of life, an expectation beyond death, or an ironic allusion to deeds.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q09/p1", "position": "He imagines wealth will prevent death and keep him alive in this world.", "reasons": "Muqātil says this lasts until wealth is spent, though neither wealth nor children can immortalize him. Al-Ṭabarī ties the illusion to amassed, counted and withheld money. Al-Zajjāj describes acting like a rich person who never expects death. Al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, Quṭb and others link it to trusting money against danger; Quṭb adds imagined escape from God's decree and judgment. Ibn ʿĀshūr says worldly survival is the hoarder's highest wish because he denies an eternal life beyond it. Al-Ālūsī allows a literal delusion caused by arrogance, distraction from judgment, or belief that material causes and wealth control health and safety. Al-Ṭabrisī says he behaves this way despite knowing everyone dies."}, {"id": "104:3/q09/p2", "position": "His wealth gives him long hopes or distracts him, so he lives as if death will never come.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan's reading reported by al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī connects this to heedlessness and distant wishes; al-Ḥasan remarks that certain death seems doubtful to people. Al-Bayḍāwī distinguishes attachment, distraction and long hopes. Al-Bursevī and Ibn ʿĀshūr say the claim is figurative, not anyone's real conviction; al-Ālūsī calls it a representational metaphor. Al-Biqāʿī says the sinner turns from God toward fleeting pleasures. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an emphatic simile satirizing greed. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī links earthly attachment and perceived self-sufficiency to boundless wants, tyranny and superiority (96:6–7)."}, {"id": "104:3/q09/p3", "position": "He thinks his wealth will lengthen his lifespan.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima gives the explicit extension of lifespan; the same report recurs through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Māwardī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Durr."}, {"id": "104:3/q09/p4", "position": "Wealth has sustained and protected his life, so he supposes it will continue to do so.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls wealth the substance and support of life; Abū Ḥayyān says it has maintaine

Al-Ālūsī calls this reading very far-fetched and notes that another scholar did not treat it as independent."}, {"id": "104:3/q09/p6", "position": "His lasting buildings, planting and landworks show an expectation of prolonged life or remembrance.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites fortified homes, trees and land development; al-Rāzī specifies brick and plaster and adds the wish to be remembered after death. {"id": "104:3/q10", "question": "How does the verse's immortality language work as figurative speech?", "turns_on": "Whether the sentence reports belief or exaggerates behavior into a claim.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q10/p1", "position": "It portrays the hoarder's conduct as though money had made him immortal.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls it representational metaphor and Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an emphatic simile; he says nobody actually thinks wealth literally immortalizes. ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī's comparison theory explains the force: 'like a lion' assigns a measured share of a common quality, while 'the lion' maximizes it; the lion's naming rests chiefly on courage. He distinguishes identity between two names from asserted complete likeness; complete likeness borrows force from identity because at different times the viewer might think he sees the same thing. Applying 'he himself' to the lion comparison suppresses differences and heightens the shared quality."}, {"id": "104:3/q10/p2", "position": "He may literally hold the delusion that money grants immortality.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī allows literal belief from arrogance, preoccupation with accumulation, neglect of the coming terrors, or trusting visible causes and wealth for life and health."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q11", "question": "What does the wealth signify inwardly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q11/p1", "position": "It is a hoard of blameworthy morals and low qualities.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī relays al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya: the person treats this hoard as provision for stages of the afterlife and entry into God's presence. {"id": "104:3/q12", "question": "What reports describe the man's wealth or conduct?", "turns_on": "The reports give distinct narratives and conflicting dinar amounts; no note resolves the amounts.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q12/p1", "position": "He boasted his wealth could provision Quraysh without running out, then counted it after a warning and provoked revelation.", "reasons": "Muqātil says he swore he could distribute wealth across Quraysh while alive without depleting it and challenged poverty; when told that its Giver could remove it, he counted his possessions and told Muḥammad that even if all were bread it would not run out. Sūrat al-Humazah was then revealed."}, {"id": "104:3/q12/p2", "position": "Al-Akhnas owned four thousand dinars.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān report this amount, while also transmitting a different figure."}, {"id": "104:3/q12/p3", "position": "Al-Akhnas owned ten thousand dinars.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and Abū Ḥayyān also report this amount; the two figures are alternatives."}, {"id": "104:3/q12/p4", "position": "A rich man told al-Ḥasan he saved thousands against hardship, rulers, calamities and poverty.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan replied that the man would leave the money to people who would neither thank him nor excuse him."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q13", "question": "Whom does this portrayal target?", "turns_on": "Whether the sketch designates a moral type, contemporary polytheists, or hypocrites.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q13/p1", "position": "A type of wealthy, self-reliant sinner who hoards and mocks.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum calls him a prototypical sinner whose unfounded trust in money fuels accumulation and antisocial conduct. Asad treats the hoarding attitude as blameworthy alongside slander; the Study Quran says the sūrah concerns torment for hoarders."}, {"id": "104:3/q13/p2", "position": "Actual polytheists who mocked the Messenger and believers.", "reasons": "Quṭb infers this from the severe warning, but considers reports naming particular individuals unreliable."}, {"id": "104:3/q13/p3", "position": "Hypocrites absorbed by money and the pleasures it purchases.", "reasons": "Islahi says their conduct reveals an attachment to this world's pleasures and contradicts belief in the Hereafter."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q14", "question": "What does this claim teach about wealth and enduring life?", "turns_on": "The notes develop both the false promise of wealth and the conduct it fosters.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q14/p1", "position": "Wealth cannot secure permanence; lasting life comes through faith, knowledge, virtue, righteous deeds and afterlife striving.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites ʿAlī: wealth keepers die while scholars remain through time. Al-Qāshānī says bodily riches perish but knowledge and spiritual virtues last. Elmalılı invokes faith in truth, knowledge and righteous action and the preceding sūrah. Ibn ʿĀshūr says hoarding withholds God's due in spending and zakāt. Islahi argues recognition of life's brevity would redirect spending and competition to the Hereafter; he cites Jesus' teaching that the heart follows where one keeps wealth. Bint al-Shāṭi says the Qurʾān reserves real eternity for the afterlife (21:34, 21:8, 26:129)."}, {"id": "104:3/q14/p2", "position": "Attachment to money breeds false self-sufficiency, greed and contempt for others.", "reasons": "Quṭb links counting and savoring money to verbal and gestural mockery; he says Islam forbids such faultfinding. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 96:6–7 on self-sufficiency producing rebellion. Asad describes material acquisition becoming almost religious and displacing spiritual concerns; Islahi says the direction of one's life reveals whether this world or the next is its destination."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q15", "question": "How does the next rebuke answer the claimed immortality?", "turns_on": "Whether kallā primarily negates his delusion or affirms the following sworn threat.", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q15/p1", "position": "Kallā declares the claim false and rebukes the hoarder.", "reasons": "ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allāh, client of Ghufra, says God's kallā marks the hearer wrong. Al-Biqāʿī says he dies like every creature; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the oath-emphasizing lām promises he will be cast into al-Ḥuṭama. Al-Bursevī also allows a rebuke of the earlier mockery; Ibn ʿĀshūr connects it to failure to spend and pay zakāt. Ibn Qutayba explicitly says kallā rejects wealth's supposed power to immortalize because the man will be cast into the Crusher."}, {"id": "104:3/q15/p2", "position": "Kallā means 'indeed' and introduces the force of an implied oath.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the lām of layunbadhanna answers this implied oath. Al-Bursevī also permits the oath connection."}]}
{"id": "104:3/q16", "question": "How does the punishment reverse the man's expectation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "104:3/q16/p1", "position": "The supposedly permanent rich mocker is thrown into crushing Fire and confined.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash says both man and wealth are cast into the Crusher. Quṭb sees a measured reversal: a rich scoffer expecting permanence is discarded, crushed in God's Fire, burned in the heart that generated pride, then confined without aid like a tied animal; sound pattern and progression from threat through question to explanation magnify it. Corpus Coranicum says verse 4 counters his imagined immortality through the root h-t-m. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says Ḥuṭama intensifies crushing, may suggest eating, and is explained as God's kindled Fire; the Study Quran compares hoarded gold and silver branding owners in 9:34–35, alongside 70:18. Ibn Qutayba connects the promised casting into the Crusher directly to the denial that wealth makes its owner immortal."}]}

{"id": "11:114/q01", "question": "What does it mean to establish prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q01/p1", "position": "Perform the prescribed prayers fully, with their required acts and at their appointed times.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi and Ibn al-Jawzi specify complete bowing and prostration. Alusi includes regular observance or prayer at the beginning of its time. Jishumi says the verse fixes times generally while the Prophet explained details; Asad and Qurtubi likewise refer forms and exact times to prophetic teaching."}, {"id": "11:114/q01/p2", "position": "Maintain prayer continuously, evenly, or at its best times.", "reasons": "These are alternative glosses reported by al-Tabrisi and Abu Hayyan; al-Alusi also reports regular maintenance and beginning-of-time performance."}, {"id": "11:114/q01/p3", "position": "Fill one's time with obligatory and voluntary worship or remembrance.", "reasons": "Sufi authorities take the command to cover all time. Asad extends its stress on prayer to remembrance throughout waking life. Bursevi allows work, human needs, and restorative sleep."}, {"id": "11:114/q01/p4", "position": "The five prayers close the five sensory doors and restore presence with God.", "reasons": "Qashani says the senses veil the heart; praying at day edges preserves gathered light through intervening times (23:9), while night wakefulness refines powers drawn toward sleep."}, {"id": "11:114/q01/p5", "position": "Prayer is the foremost worship after faith and a refuge in hardship.", "reasons": "Razi relates its placement after steadfastness to its rank; Biqai calls it the broadest aid to uprightness; Qurtubi reports the Prophet turned to prayer when troubled."}]}
{"id": "11:114/q02", "question": "Which prayers are at the two ends of the day?", "turns_on": "Whether dawn and sunset count within daytime, and whether the latter half of the day can contain both Zuhr and Asr as an end.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q02/p1", "position": "Fajr at the first end and Zuhr and Asr at the second.", "reasons": "Wahidi prefers Zajjaj: Maghrib belongs to night. Zamakhshari calls Zuhr and Asr evening prayers; Elmalili calls them the after-noon division. Tabatabai says the five-prayer report points to before and after noon. Qurtubi reports Ibn Atiyya's choice. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views. Al-Damghani also identifies dawn, noon, and afternoon and notes 20:130."}, {"id": "11:114/q02/p2", "position": "Fajr and Asr.", "reasons": "Razi says sunrise and sunset mark opposite edges, leaving Maghrib to night; he parallels 20:130. Abu Hayyan says each boundary belongs to what it bounds and cites fasting from dawn. Biqai notes morning and afternoon prayer before the Night Journey. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views. Razi says Abu Hanifa inferred later performance of Fajr and Asr near the boundaries."}, {"id": "11:114/q02/p3", "position": "Fajr and Maghrib.", "reasons": "Tabari argues that all agree on Fajr and that Maghrib alone supplies the opposite end; Wahidi says the apparent wording supports it. Tabrisi says Zuhr and Asr are obvious daytime prayers or specified by 17:78. Qurtubi defends dawn as daytime from fasting law but retains the sunset objection. Kuranyolu defines day as dawn to sunset. Ibn al-Jawzi reports al-Dahhak accepts all three second-end views."}, {"id": "11:114/q02/p4", "position": "Zuhr and Asr are the two boundaries; Fajr is grouped with night prayers.", "reasons": "Some connect this grouping with quiet versus loud recitation. Elmalili argues dawn is the day's root and noon and afternoon its two prominent parts; the night set of Maghrib, Isha and Fajr gives five prayers, with 17:78 and 20:130."}, {"id": "11:114/q02/p5", "position": "Fajr and Isha.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports this from Mujahid."}, {"id": "11:114/q02/p6", "position": "Fajr and Zuhr at one end, Asr and Maghrib at the other.", "reasons": "Wahidi and Baghawi attribute this division to Muqatil."}, {"id": "11:114/q02/p7", "position": "The first end is Fajr, while the evening end remains disputed.", "reasons": "Tabari says all agree on Fajr but differ about evening; Ibn al-Jawzi reports the majority agrees, but notes Ibn Jarir gives Zuhr instead. Qurtubi transmits Mawardi's claimed agreement and qualifies it by the Zuhr/Asr view. Asad gives the literal wording, 'the two ends of the day.'"}]}

{"id": "11:114/q07", "question": "What does زلفا mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q07/p1", "position": "Near or successive hours, stages, or portions of the night; singular zulfa.", "reasons": "Akhfash lists zulfat and zulf as other plurals. {"id": "11:114/q08", "question": "How is زلفا read?", "turns_on": "The vowel on lam and whether the form is a plural, collective, or singular.", "positions": [{"id": "11:114/q08/p1", "position": "Zulafan, with damma on zay and fatha on lam, a plural of zulfa.", "reasons": "Tabari prefers this because Isha follows portions of the night; Sam in calls it the common reading, and Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan the majority reading.
